newsitem.title: JAPAN: Asian Metals - Japan market eyes LME copper rally.
newsitem.headline: Asian Metals - Japan market eyes LME copper rally.

text.p: Japan's metal markets are monitoring volatile copper prices on the London Metal Exchange after their recent rally, although no near-term impact is expected on Japanese consumption or premiums, market sources said on Wednesday.
"It won't affect premiums much," an official at one end-user said. "For the first part of the month, users are taking a wait-and-see stance."
On Monday, three-month LME copper spiked to a 2 1/2-month high of $2,165 a tonne but quickly dipped back below $2,100.
In early business in London on Wednesday, three-month copper was holding slightly above $2,050.

Market sources said Japan's physical copper market remained relatively tight. One added that scrap supplies may increase if prices remain at recent higher levels, although he was sceptical that three-month copper could hold above $2,000 in the intermediate to longer term.

Also catching the market's attention was a water shortage in the area surrounding Japan's 250,000 tonne-per-year capacity Onahama copper refinery, with one trader saying output could be affected next month if water levels remain low.
Aluminium traders said the spot market was quiet as the recent firmer trend on the LME and a slip in the yen against the dollar made prices less attractive to Japanese end-users.

Premiums were steady to slightly weaker, after negotiations last week and the week before with Western producers set premiums for October-December contracts around $62 a tonne over LME cash prices, a drop of about three dollars from the previous quarter.
A source at a major trade house said he had seen no offers, however, for premiums below $60, and several traders expected them to remain in the $60 to $65 area in the near term.

The zinc market remained quiet, with long-term contracts continuing to meet most domestic needs. One trader noted rising input costs in China helping to keep metal from that market too pricey to interest Japanese users.

He added that Japanese users are beginning to consider their needs for next spring's GSP buying and appear likely to reduce their purchases from this year's levels. "They bought too much last time," he said.
